_comment: Account sync wire format and merge rules (Phase 2 of the accounts work),
consumed by ALL THREE ports: the Swift harness (MorseKitCheck), android
SyncWireTest and desktop SyncWireTest. Data, not code: see CLAUDE.md's
two-ports rule.
Source of truth: the API contract in the N9HO/another-morse-trainer-accounts
README (sections 7 and 9). Expected values are derived from that contract
and the rules below, not captured from any port's encoder. Change this file
only together with that README, and say so in the commit.
Wire rules:
- `date` is epoch MILLISECONDS as an integer. iOS JSONEncoder's default Date
strategy (seconds since 2001) must never reach the wire.
- The apps keep TTRs in seconds; on the wire `fastestTtrMs`, `medianTtrMs`
and per-character `medianTtrMs` are whole milliseconds, round(seconds *
1000). Decoding divides by 1000. No value here sits on a .5 boundary in
binary floating point (0.3895 would: 0.3895 * 1000 is exactly 389.5).
- `durationSeconds` is a number, unchanged.
- `id` is the record's UUID, lowercase on the wire.
- An absent value is JSON null, never the -1 sentinel the Kotlin ports use
in their own storage.
- `schemaVersion` is 1.
- `mode` on the wire is the canonical mode id: the iOS TrainingMode raw
value. `modeIds.kotlin` maps every string Android and desktop record to
it (all 25, both ways). iOS sends its raw value unchanged. Decoding a wire
id that a Kotlin port does not know keeps the wire id as the local mode.
Merge rules are under `merge`; each scenario names its inputs and the
expected result.

pkce._comment: RFC 7636 Appendix B. challenge = base64url(SHA-256(ASCII(verifier))), no padding.

client._comment: verify/start `client` per port; `platform` is one of these by device.

session._comment: One record with every field populated. `local` is the port's own record in seconds; `localMode` per port. Encoding `local` must give exactly `wire` (key order free). Decoding `wire` gives back `local` with the id lowercased and each TTR at millisecond precision (0.2124 s comes back as 0.212 s): the ms rounding is the only loss.

legacySession._comment: A record from before speeds, TTRs, duration and score were kept: every optional value absent, both speeds 0, a passive mode. Its wire form carries explicit nulls and empty lists.

days._comment: POST /v1/sync/days body: THIS DEVICE'S OWN per-day seconds (see merge.deviceDays), local calendar days as the ledger keys them, whole seconds. Never the adopted, account-wide ledger. A day with 0 seconds is a practice day with no timed session (a Daily Dit guess).

state._comment: PUT /v1/sync/state. The five keys that exist in all three trees, each with ONE wire shape. `kotlin` gives the Android/desktop stored form each key is translated from; iOS stores Codable blobs whose fields already match the wire names except where noted. `characters.stage` is lowercase on the wire (iOS raw values); the Kotlin enum names are capitalised. `journey.completed` is ascending. `characters` never carries the opt-in punctuation (MorseCode.pickablePunctuation: . , /): each device's own punctuation setting decides those, so they are dropped from activeCharacters and exposedCharacters when encoding, and a received ladder keeps the device's own punctuation entries (see `charactersPunctuation`). Otherwise two devices with different punctuation settings would rewrite each other's ladder on every launch.

charactersPunctuation._comment: Applying a received ladder: the received Koch characters, in the order received, then the device's own opt-in punctuation that was in its active (exposed) set, in its local order. Stage and pin come from the wire as usual.

_comment: Settings sync: the training preferences that exist on all three apps with the same meaning, each its own PUT /v1/sync/state key (`setting.` + name), so last-writer-wins never loses a change to one setting because another changed elsewhere. Four keys are small groups whose fields constrain each other and are set together: `speed` (the effective speed may not exceed the character speed), `rapidFireWordLength`, `pileupCallerSpeed` and `pileupDelay` (min <= max).
Source of truth: the accounts README section 9, 'Settings keys'. Values derived from that spec, not captured from a port.

Every value has ONE wire shape (`kind` below). Wire enum strings are the iOS raw values; `kotlin` lists the Android/desktop local values in the same order as `values` (enum constant names, or the stored value where the Kotlin port keeps one).

Kinds: bool (JSON true/false); int {min,max} (any JSON number, rounded to the nearest whole number, then clamped); number {min,max,step} (clamped, then rounded to the nearest multiple of step; step 0.1 means one decimal place); enum {values} (a string from values); intChoice {values} (a number, rounded, that must be one of values); members {values,minCount} (a list of strings from values, unknown ones dropped, duplicates dropped, in the order of values; fewer than minCount left is unusable); text {maxLength,transform}; words {maxCount,maxLength}; range {min:[lo,hi], max:[lo,hi], whole} (an object {min,max}, each clamped to its bounds, whole numbers when `whole`, else one decimal place; then a max below min is raised to min); speed (an object {characterWpm int 15..60, farnsworth bool, effectiveWpm int 8..60}; effectiveWpm is then lowered to characterWpm if above it).

text transforms: callsign = trim, uppercase, keep only A-Z 0-9 and /, then the first maxLength; state = uppercase, keep only A-Z, then the first maxLength; trim = trim whitespace, then the first maxLength characters; id = unchanged when it matches ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{0,64}$, else unusable.
words: each entry trimmed and uppercased; empty ones dropped; longer than maxLength cut to maxLength; duplicates dropped keeping the first; the first maxCount kept.

Normalising: a value received from the account, AND each value this device sends, goes through its kind's rule. An unusable value (wrong JSON type, an unknown enum string, a missing field) is ignored: the local setting stands and nothing is stamped. A key this app does not know is ignored. Each app also applies its own input rules after (the custom-word parser, for one).
A setting a platform does not have is not here: only settings all three apps have. Device-specific settings never sync (accounts README section 9's 'not synced' list).

normalize._comment: `out` is the normalised value; null means unusable (ignored: the local setting stands). Applied to received values and to every value a device sends.

isDefault._comment: Whether a value, once normalised, equals the key's default. A never-stamped setting at its default is never sent (see stamping).

_comment: Settings follow the progress stamping rules (merge.state) with one difference: a setting is only ever sent once it has a stamp, and only a user's change, or a first sign-in with a non-default value, gives it one. So a fresh install's defaults never reach the account, and a device whose setting was never changed takes the account's value whatever its stamp.
1. A user's change while signed in stamps the key now (only keys whose normalised wire value changed). Signed out, nothing is stamped.

2. First sign-in: a never-stamped setting whose value differs from the default is stamped 0 and sent, so it fills a key the account lacks and never outranks one it has; a never-stamped setting AT its default is not stamped and not sent; a stamped one goes with its stamp.
3. An unstamped setting is never sent, and any value the account has for it is applied.

4. A received value strictly newer than the local stamp is normalised and applied; the stamp becomes the received one. Applying it is not a change of ours: it never stamps, and neither does anything the apply changes in turn.

5. A key the server rejects (`rejected` in the reply: until the accounts Worker knows the settings keys, every one is `unknown key`) leaves the queue like any answered key; the value and its stamp stay, nothing backs off, and the next state push sends it again.

userChange._comment: Signed in, every key stamped as in firstSignIn.expectedStamps. At `now` the user sets tonePitch to 720 and saves; the speed group is saved unchanged. Only tonePitch is restamped.

outOfRangeReceived._comment: A newer value from another platform outside this app's range is clamped on the way in, applied, and takes the received stamp; it is not restamped (the clamped value goes back only after a later change of ours).

unusableReceived._comment: A newer value this app cannot read keeps the local value AND the local stamp.

sessions._comment: Pulled or snapshot records are inserted when their id (compared lowercase) is not already local; an existing local record is never replaced. Then sort newest date first (equal dates: id ascending) and keep the newest `limit`. `limit` is the app's SessionHistory limit (100); 4 here to show the cap.

aggregates._comment: After every successful push or pull reply that carries `stats`, these local lifetime counters are REPLACED by the server's, so a fresh install shows totals beyond the 100 rows it holds. bestTTR goes from ms to seconds; personalBests replaces the whole bests map. Mode keys here are canonical ids, as on the wire: a port that keys its bests by its own mode string (the Kotlin titles) maps them through `modeIds` on the way in.

ledger._comment: The server's summed per-day figures are adopted into the DISPLAYED ledger day by day; local days the reply does not mention are kept. The app's 400-day cap then applies as it already does. The displayed ledger is never pushed (see deviceDays).

deviceDays._comment: Each device keeps its OWN per-day seconds apart from the displayed ledger, and pushes only those. The server keeps the larger figure per device-day and sums devices, so pushing an adopted (already summed) figure would count the other devices twice. The own record grows with every local session (same day key and seconds the ledger records), is seeded once from the local ledger the first time the device ever signs in (before any adoption), survives sign-out, and is never touched by adoption.
deviceDays.pushBodyNote: Only days changed since the last successful push go out (the outbox's day entries); each carries the device's own figure for that day.

state._comment: Per key, a reply entry replaces the local one only when its updatedAt is strictly newer; equal or older keeps local. Keys the reply omits keep local. Stamping: a key gets updatedAt = now (epoch ms) when a save changes its wire value WHILE SIGNED IN; resets never stamp. At first sign-in a key that has never been stamped goes out with updatedAt 0, so any value the account already has wins and the device's value only fills an empty account (a fresh install's onboarding defaults never overwrite real progress); a key never saved on the device is not sent at all.

outbox._comment: An outbox entry leaves only on a 2xx whose reply lists its id as accepted or skipped; a rejected id also leaves (it stays in local history). Ids not in the reply stay, in order. Order of drain: sessions oldest first in batches of up to 200, then days, then state.

cap._comment: At most `max` entries; enqueuing past it drops the oldest. 3 here to show it; the apps use 1000.

backoff._comment: Seconds before retry n (1-based): 2^n, capped at 600 (10 min). Reset to retry 1 on success, or on a foreground that syncs (a foreground held back by foregroundThrottle changes nothing, so a scheduled retry stands).

retry._comment: What the engine does with an HTTP outcome. `refresh` = refresh the token once, then retry once. If the refresh itself is refused (a 4xx), sign out; if the refresh gets no reply, a 429 or a 5xx, keep the tokens and back off, since the refresh token was not spent. `network` = no HTTP reply at all.

_comment: One authenticated request answered 401: refresh the token once, then send the request once more. Per scenario: `refresh` is the refresh's status; `retry` the second answer to the request (null: it is not sent again). `result`: ok (the 2xx reply comes back), signedOut (the tokens are cleared and the device is signed out, banner and all), backoff (the tokens are kept; try later). `tokens` after: rotated (the refresh's new pair), kept (the old pair), cleared. `requests` counts the request itself, `refreshes` the refresh calls.

The rule this pins: a 401 on the retry, straight after a refresh that worked, means this device's sign-in was revoked. It signs out; it is never an ordinary error to back off on, and it never refreshes a second time. README sections 5 and 10.

A return to the foreground (desktop: the window regaining focus; on every app launch is the first foreground) syncs only when at least `minIntervalSeconds` have passed since the last foreground sync that ran. A full sync is several requests and focus can change many times a minute; this keeps the Worker's rate limit (429) out of reach. A held-back foreground does NOTHING: no sync, no backoff reset, and the clock does not move.

Only `throttled` triggers are gated, and only they move the clock. Sync now, the push after a local change, the sign-in's first sync and a backoff retry always run and never move it. The clock is kept in memory, so a cold launch always syncs. A clock that reads earlier than the last foreground sync (the wall clock was set back) syncs.
`sequence` runs in order against one fresh throttle: `atSeconds` is when each trigger fires, `syncs` whether it runs. Idea from PR #336.
